title: The Great
synopsis: You arrived in Russia at fifteen, married a man-child emperor at sixteen, and by autumn you have decided, politely, to take the throne for yourself. Huzzah.

nodes.text: Peter is asleep, snoring like a stabbed bear, with one foot on your pillow. The candles are guttering. You stare at the ceiling and decide, in the politest possible terms, to overthrow him by spring.

choices.text: Plan it carefully — alone, for now
choices.consequence: Conspiracies of one are the only safe kind. You commit to plan it carefully — alone, for now. The road to The Library is now open, and at least two people are already preparing to misunderstand why.

choices.text: Find one ally tomorrow morning
choices.consequence: Even queens need a witness. You commit to find one ally tomorrow morning. The road to Marial, Maid and Mind is now open, and at least two people are already preparing to misunderstand why.

nodes.text: You sneak into the imperial library and read every book Peter has banned. Most are merely better than him. A few are dangerous. You take notes in a tiny hand and hide them in a hollowed prayer book. Huzzah.

choices.text: Lean into the danger of new ideas
choices.consequence: Reading is the first regicide. You lean into the danger of new ideas. It gets you to Orlo's Eyes, though not with the dignity or plausible deniability you would have preferred.

choices.text: Choose which ideas to share, and with whom
choices.consequence: Strategy in the margins. You commit to choose which ideas to share, and with whom. The road to Peter's Cruelty is now open, and at least two people are already preparing to misunderstand why.

nodes.text: Marial, who was a lady before Peter's father exiled her family to scrubbing floors, eyes you sideways and says, 'You're not as dim as you look.' This is the warmest thing anyone has said to you in Russia.

choices.text: Recruit her openly into your plan
choices.consequence: An enemy of the same enemy is an ally. You recruit her openly into your plan. It gets you to Orlo's Eyes, though not with the dignity or plausible deniability you would have preferred.

choices.text: Test her loyalty with smaller secrets first
choices.consequence: Friendship is also a vetting process. You commit to test her loyalty with smaller secrets first. The road to Peter's Cruelty is now open, and at least two people are already preparing to misunderstand why.

nodes.text: Orlo, an advisor with very small spectacles and very large fears, has been writing pamphlets nobody reads. He thinks Russia could be reformed. He also, you suspect, thinks he is about to faint. To choose “Promise him reform in exchange for help” means meeting The Patriarch; “Recruit him by terrifying him politely” sends you toward The Army instead.

choices.text: Promise him reform in exchange for help
choices.consequence: Marry his ideas to your appetite. You commit to promise him reform in exchange for help. The road to The Patriarch is now open, and at least two people are already preparing to misunderstand why.

choices.text: Recruit him by terrifying him politely
choices.consequence: Fear is an underrated motivator. You recruit him by terrifying him politely. It gets you to The Army, though not with the dignity or plausible deniability you would have preferred.

nodes.text: Peter shoots a bear that lived in a garden because it was 'in his sun.' Then he weeps about it, kindly, for an hour. He is awful in nine ways at once, including charming. You write it all down.

choices.text: Use his contradictions against him
choices.consequence: A man who cries and shoots is a man with seams. You choose to use his contradictions against him. By The Patriarch, the plan will either look inspired or become a story told at your expense for years.

choices.text: Pity him just enough to stay safe
choices.consequence: Tenderness can be camouflage. You choose to pity him just enough to stay safe. By The Army, the plan will either look inspired or become a story told at your expense for years.

nodes.text: Archbishop Archie — perfumed, sly, dangerous — invites you to chapel. Faith in Russia is a sword pretending to be a candle. He smiles. He wants to know whose side God will be on this winter. Choose “Promise the church it will keep its lands” and The Salon comes into view; choose “Promise the church one reform at a time” and the road bends toward The Hunt.

choices.text: Promise the church it will keep its lands
choices.consequence: Faith is the largest landlord. You commit to promise the church it will keep its lands. The road to The Salon is now open, and at least two people are already preparing to misunderstand why.

choices.text: Promise the church one reform at a time
choices.consequence: Compromise as a velvet glove. You promise the church one reform at a time. It gets you to The Hunt, though not with the dignity or plausible deniability you would have preferred.

nodes.text: General Velementov, drunk by lunch and brilliant by accident, is the closest thing the army has to a brain. He has stopped believing in Peter. He has not, yet, started believing in you. “Charm Velementov into your circle” opens the route to The Salon. “Threaten Velementov into your circle” changes the terms and carries you toward The Hunt.

choices.text: Charm Velementov into your circle
choices.consequence: Soldiers follow conviction, not titles. You commit to charm Velementov into your circle. The road to The Salon is now open, and at least two people are already preparing to misunderstand why.

choices.text: Threaten Velementov into your circle
choices.consequence: Pride wounded can be useful. You threaten Velementov into your circle. It gets you to The Hunt, though not with the dignity or plausible deniability you would have preferred.

nodes.text: You start a salon — books, ideas, women allowed to speak. The court calls it a scandal. The women, quietly and quickly, call it church. Half your future ministers are taking notes in the corner. “Use the salon to seed your reforms” opens the route to Smallpox. “Use the salon to spot your loyalists” changes the terms and carries you toward Peter's Mother's Portrait.

choices.text: Use the salon to seed your reforms
choices.consequence: Ideas pour out of rooms that are too small to hold them. You choose to use the salon to seed your reforms. By Smallpox, the plan will either look inspired or become a story told at your expense for years.

choices.text: Use the salon to spot your loyalists
choices.consequence: Talent reveals itself when it feels welcome. You use the salon to spot your loyalists. It gets you to Peter's Mother's Portrait, though not with the dignity or plausible deniability you would have preferred.

nodes.text: Peter takes you hunting and tells you, drunk, that he 'sometimes' worries you might be cleverer than him. He laughs. He waits. You realize you are choosing your own life with the next sentence. The paths divide here: “Flatter him brilliantly and live” leads into Smallpox, while “Tell him a smaller version of the truth” makes Peter's Mother's Portrait the next reckoning.

choices.text: Flatter him brilliantly and live
choices.consequence: A clever woman in this room is a dead woman without a smile. You flatter him brilliantly and live. It gets you to Smallpox, though not with the dignity or plausible deniability you would have preferred.

choices.text: Tell him a smaller version of the truth
choices.consequence: Honesty in homeopathic doses. You tell him a smaller version of the truth. It gets you to Peter's Mother's Portrait, though not with the dignity or plausible deniability you would have preferred.

nodes.text: An outbreak. The court panics. You have read about a procedure — inoculation — that everyone considers heresy. You could save thousands. You could also be torn apart in the street for it. To choose “Inoculate yourself first, publicly” means meeting The Coup, Planned; “Quietly inoculate the children of allies” sends you toward Betrayal instead.

choices.text: Inoculate yourself first, publicly
choices.consequence: Lead with your own veins. You choose to inoculate yourself first, publicly. By The Coup, Planned, the plan will either look inspired or become a story told at your expense for years.

choices.text: Quietly inoculate the children of allies
choices.consequence: Save who you can; survive to save more. You choose to quietly inoculate the children of allies. By Betrayal, the plan will either look inspired or become a story told at your expense for years.

nodes.text: Peter speaks to a portrait of his mother as if she could answer. He is, terribly, a small boy in a large hat. You find that tonight, against your better judgement, you don't want to kill him. You want to fix him.

choices.text: Resolve to depose him without killing him
choices.consequence: Mercy is also a strategy. You choose to resolve to depose him without killing him. By The Coup, Planned, the plan will either look inspired or become a story told at your expense for years.

choices.text: Resolve to depose him fully; sentiment is fatal
choices.consequence: Soft hearts make short reigns. You resolve to depose him fully; sentiment is fatal. It gets you to Betrayal, though not with the dignity or plausible deniability you would have preferred.

nodes.text: In the deep cold of a December night you and Marial and Orlo and Velementov bend over a map of the Winter Palace. You count guards. You count corridors. You count, mostly, the people you have to ask to risk their lives.

choices.text: Strike at the Christmas ball
choices.consequence: Spectacle covers footsteps. You commit to strike at the Christmas ball. The road to The Ballroom is now open, and at least two people are already preparing to misunderstand why.

choices.text: Strike at dawn after a long quiet day
choices.consequence: Boredom is the best disguise. You choose to strike at dawn after a long quiet day. By Dawn Move, the plan will either look inspired or become a story told at your expense for years.

nodes.text: One of your circle has wavered — Archbishop Archie, maybe, or someone smaller. A letter has reached Peter that mentions your name with a verb he won't like. You have hours, not days. The paths divide here: “Move the coup forward to tonight” leads into The Ballroom, while “Bluff your way through it and buy time” makes Dawn Move the next reckoning.

choices.text: Move the coup forward to tonight
choices.consequence: Improvise or die polite. You choose to move the coup forward to tonight. By The Ballroom, the plan will either look inspired or become a story told at your expense for years.

choices.text: Bluff your way through it and buy time
choices.consequence: Charm has saved smaller empires. You commit to bluff your way through it and buy time. The road to Dawn Move is now open, and at least two people are already preparing to misunderstand why.

nodes.text: Candles, mirrors, three orchestras, the whole court turning like a slow gilded wheel. Peter is dancing badly. Velementov is at the doors. You smile. You step toward the center of the floor. The paths divide here: “Make a public speech declaring the new order” leads into Peter, Cornered, while “Strike quietly first, speak after” makes The Crown the next reckoning.

choices.text: Make a public speech declaring the new order
choices.consequence: Theater is power's first language. You make a public speech declaring the new order. It gets you to Peter, Cornered, though not with the dignity or plausible deniability you would have preferred.

choices.text: Strike quietly first, speak after
choices.consequence: Surgery before the announcement. You strike quietly first, speak after. It gets you to The Crown, though not with the dignity or plausible deniability you would have preferred.

nodes.text: Before sunrise your loyalists move through the palace's nervous corridors. There are surprisingly few deaths and surprisingly many men changing sides on the spot. Russia loves a winner more than a tsar. The distance between Peter, Cornered and The Crown begins with the choice between “Spare every life you can” and “Spare only the necessary ones.”

choices.text: Spare every life you can
choices.consequence: Reigns founded on mercy hold longer. You spare every life you can. It gets you to Peter, Cornered, though not with the dignity or plausible deniability you would have preferred.

choices.text: Spare only the necessary ones
choices.consequence: A wise queen knows arithmetic. You choose to spare only the necessary ones. By The Crown, the plan will either look inspired or become a story told at your expense for years.

nodes.text: He sits on the floor of his own bedroom looking up at you like a child who has lost a game whose rules he made up. 'You really did it,' he says. He sounds almost proud.

choices.text: Send him into gilded exile
choices.consequence: Keep your enemy alive and decorative. You send him into gilded exile. It gets you to The Reforms, though not with the dignity or plausible deniability you would have preferred.

choices.text: Force him to abdicate publicly
choices.consequence: Paperwork is the truest crown. You choose to force him to abdicate publicly. By A Child, the plan will either look inspired or become a story told at your expense for years.

nodes.text: Archbishop Archie, who almost betrayed you, kneels on instinct because Russia has shown him whose side God is now on. The crown is heavier than it looks. The mirror behind him reflects a woman you barely recognize.

choices.text: Wear it with steel
choices.consequence: The future is shaped by women who do not flinch. You wear it with steel. It gets you to The Reforms, though not with the dignity or plausible deniability you would have preferred.

choices.text: Wear it with care
choices.consequence: Power held lightly is held longest. You commit to wear it with care. The road to A Child is now open, and at least two people are already preparing to misunderstand why.

nodes.text: In your first hundred days you free the serfs of three provinces, build two schools, and survive four attempts on your life. Russia, baffled and delighted, calls it a beginning. You call it Tuesday. Choose “Push the reforms harder, faster” and The Long Reign comes into view; choose “Slow down to build the institutions that will outlast you” and the road bends toward Peter, Late.

choices.text: Push the reforms harder, faster
choices.consequence: Momentum is itself protection. You commit to push the reforms harder, faster. The road to The Long Reign is now open, and at least two people are already preparing to misunderstand why.

choices.text: Slow down to build the institutions that will outlast you
choices.consequence: A reform that depends on a queen dies with one. You choose to slow down to build the institutions that will outlast you. By Peter, Late, the plan will either look inspired or become a story told at your expense for years.

nodes.text: You are pregnant, possibly by Peter, possibly not. The court bets discreetly. You decide, alone in a snowed-in garden, that the child will be raised to know more languages than thrones and more books than crowns.

choices.text: Raise an heir for the new Russia
choices.consequence: Continuity is a kind of revolution. You commit to raise an heir for the new Russia. The road to The Long Reign is now open, and at least two people are already preparing to misunderstand why.

choices.text: Decline the dynasty game entirely
choices.consequence: Some empires should not be inherited. You choose to decline the dynasty game entirely. By Peter, Late, the plan will either look inspired or become a story told at your expense for years.

nodes.text: Years pass. The empire grows wider, kinder, stranger. Your enemies write books about you that are mostly lies and partly accurate. Marial has her own salon now. Orlo has stopped fainting. Velementov has, on most days, sobered up.

choices.text: Reign for as long as you live
choices.consequence: Empires are stories you keep telling. You reign for as long as you live. It gets you to Catherine the Great, though not with the dignity or plausible deniability you would have preferred.

choices.text: Abdicate to a successor on your own terms
choices.consequence: The bravest crown is the one you put down. You choose to abdicate to a successor on your own terms. By Huzzah, And Then, the plan will either look inspired or become a story told at your expense for years.

nodes.text: Years later you visit Peter in his comfortable exile — fat, sad, gardening, occasionally good. He laughs about old times. You realize, walking away, that the strangest thing about ruling Russia is that you both, somehow, won.

choices.text: Forgive him on the carriage ride home
choices.consequence: Forgiveness is the last revolution. You commit to forgive him on the carriage ride home. The road to Huzzah, And Then is now open, and at least two people are already preparing to misunderstand why.

choices.text: Keep him in his comfortable exile forever
choices.consequence: Some mercies have walls. You keep him in his comfortable exile forever. It gets you to Catherine the Great, though not with the dignity or plausible deniability you would have preferred.

nodes.text: They will call you Great. You will call you tired. The salons you started outlive you. The reforms you broke yourself on become ordinary. Somewhere in Europe a girl reads your name and decides, secretly, that she will rule too. Huzzah.

You step down on a day of your choosing, into a quiet life of books and chosen company. The crown goes onto a head that has read more books than its predecessors combined. The empire, for now, does not collapse. You take that as a win.
